newsitem.title: UK: Decommissioning row haunts N.Ireland peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Decommissioning row haunts N.Ireland peace talks.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair appeared to keep Northern Ireland's peace process on track on Monday after showdown talks with the province's Protestant leader David Trimble on the surrender of IRA arms.

Trimble pressed Blair to make clear to the guerrilla Irish Republican Army (IRA) that it must hand over some of the guns it has used in a 28-year war against British rule of Northern Ireland so that its Sinn Fein political wing could take part in the peace process.

Sinn Fein, which seeks the reunification of Ireland, says that a handover of weapons should be part of a final settlement to the conflict and that "arms decommissioning" should be left until the last item on the talks agenda.

Trimble, leader of the Ulster Unionist Party, the biggest pro-British group in Northern Ireland, emerged from hour-long talks at Blair's Downing Street residence in London saying that the session was inconclusive and that further official contact would be needed.
"There are some possibilities of progress... but the matter is not yet clear," he told waiting reporters.

Britain's Northern Ireland secretary, Mo Mowlam, who attended the London meeting, said Trimble would not follow the lead of a unionist ally and walk out of the year-long talks, which are co-sponsored by Britain and Ireland.

She said it was vital to maintain momentum in the peace process after the IRA called a ceasefire at the weekend which will permit admission of Sinn Fein to negotiations on a political settlement in September if the truce is judged genuine by Britain.

"There is no indication that the UUP were going to walk from the talks which is very useful because after the ceasefire what is important to so many people in Northern Ireland is that we do manage to move the talks process forward," she told reporters.
But a smaller group, the UK Unionist party, announced that it was pulling out of the talks in protest at what its leader, Robert McCartney, called "terror appeasement" by Britain.
It was the first time any party had quit the peace talks, which have been deadlocked for a year over the issue of "decommissioning" arms held by pro- and anti-British guerrillas.
McCartney and the Democratic Unionist Party, which meets Blair on Tuesday, say Sinn Fein should not even be admitted to the talks until its IRA allies are disarmed and disbanded.
A plenary session of the talks on Wednesday votes on Anglo-Irish proposals that decommissioning be tackled by a sub committee in parallel with political negotiations.

Trimble, the biggest voice of pro-British Protestants, fears that decommissioning will be effectively sidelined allowing Sinn Fein to negotiate with a formidable guerrilla army at its back ready to attack any settlement it does not like.
Sinn Fein's chief negotiator, Martin McGuinness, spelled out the IRA position at the weekend.
"The IRA have said that they will not decommission a single bullet and I have not heard any statement from them saying they have changed their position on that," he said.

In his first public comment on the IRA truce, Trimble was sharply critical of the government's Northern Ireland Office for proposing that Sinn Fein be allowed to take part in negotiations before the IRA hands over a single weapon.
"We are dealing with duplicity from the Northern Ireland office on a massive scale," Trimble told BBC Radio Ulster before the London meeting.

The decommissioning row overshadowed Sunday's IRA ceasefire and Sinn Fein's admission for the first time to Stormont buildings, the former seat of a Northern Ireland legislature where the peace talks are taking place.

Gerry Kelly, a convicted IRA bomber who is now a Sinn Fein official, arrived to occupy offices Britain set aside for his party but refused to allow it to use until the IRA renewed a broken August 1994 ceasefire at the weekend.

Kelly was convicted of carrying out the bombing of Britain's Old Bailey court complex in 1972. He escaped from a British jail and was extradited from the Netherlands before returning to Belfast to represent Sinn Fein.
He and an aide checked out office space and equipment briefly. "We came this morning to get our office in order. We had a fairly long meeting with Stormont administrative officials,"
Kelly played own McCartney's walkout. "People should talk and the more people who stay to talk, the better it is for the people of Ireland. We hope the Unionists will join us."
He also held brief talks with Irish Foreign MInister Ray Burke and expected to meet the talks' chairman, former U.S. senator George Mitchell, later.
